In the context of the contextual bandit problem, where agents receive data-driven recommendations and must select actions to optimize reward outcomes, we examine the issue of reward misestimation stemming from incentives. We propose a new method, called iML, which addresses this problem by utilizing a neural network to correct for reward bias during estimation. By leveraging an additional neural network to predict the biased rewards from observed actions and context, iML estimates unbiased rewards. We demonstrate the efficacy of iML in both offline and online settings, showcasing its ability to outperform existing unbiased estimation methods, and provide theoretical support for its use in the contextual bandit problem. We also show that iML can be integrated into online learning algorithms, such as LinUCB, to improve performance. Experimental results confirm that iML outperforms or matches the performance of unbiased estimation methods, and provides a significant advantage over uncorrected estimators. We have developed a theoretical framework to study the thermodynamic properties of strange stars at high temperatures, using a relativistic mean-field approach. Our model incorporates the Zha-Tang parameterization, which accurately represents the equation of state for neutron star matter, and we've applied this to calculate key parameters such as the star's mass, radius, surface gravity, and surface redshift at various temperatures. Notably, our results indicate that the star's mass and radius decrease with temperature, and we've also found that the surface gravity and redshift increase with temperature. Furthermore, we've discovered that the star can reach a critical temperature above which it becomes unstable and cannot maintain hydrostatic equilibrium. Our findings align with previous research on the maximum mass and radius of neutron stars, and we've also compared our results with those from other theoretical models. This work has significant implications for understanding the behavior of strange stars in the context of astrophysical observations. We investigate the issue of mode collapse in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) by examining the training process of the generator. Our research reveals that mode collapse occurs when the generator's parameters converge to a point where small changes result in significant alterations to the output. This'stiffness' is quantified through the Hessian matrix's eigenvalues, specifically its largest and second-largest values. Our study involves conducting a series of experiments on various datasets and GAN architectures to validate this theory. The results show that mode collapse occurs when the second-largest Hessian eigenvalue approaches zero and the largest one is extremely high. To address mode collapse, we propose a straightforward yet effective approach: incorporating a small amount of random noise into the generator during training. This technique is applied to multiple GAN architectures and yields substantial improvements in mode collapse, as evidenced by the Fr\'echet Inception Distance scores. Moreover, our method is efficient and can be implemented with minimal computational resources, making it an attractive solution for real-world applications. The code and experimental results are publicly available for review. Overall, our research provides a new understanding of mode collapse and offers a practical solution to mitigate it. Our findings indicate that this trade-off is a key consideration in the analysis of complex networks, and that our method may be a useful tool in this endeavor. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach called Merging Task Indicators via Improving Joint Predictability (MITIP), which aims to enhance the mergeability of task indicators by improving the joint predictability of tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that MITIP outperforms existing methods on both artificial and real-world datasets, and we also showcase its ability to handle complex multi-task learning scenarios. We've developed a system that automatically corrects grammatical errors in text, such as blog posts and news articles, by using a model that can identify and correct mistakes without altering the original text's meaning. Our model, which is trained on a vast dataset of text with minor grammatical errors, achieves impressive results in correcting grammatical errors, with notable accuracy in detecting significant mistakes that impact comprehension. However, it struggles with minor errors that don't affect meaning, and we've found that models trained on a mix of minor and major errors perform better than those trained on minor errors alone. We demonstrate that Mandell's inverse K-theory categories are closed under 
products of categories, thereby confirming a key conjecture of Charles Rezk. 
Additionally, we establish the perturbed linearization functor has a left adjoint, 
and that the Mandell inverse K-theory of a symmetric monoidal category is closed 
under taking closed symmetric monoidal algebras. Furthermore, we show that the 
Mandell inverse K-theory of a monoidal category is left adjoint to a certain 
functor extending the free monoidification functor. These results are achieved by 
utilizing a new, simplified definition of the Mandell inverse K-theory, which 
builds upon the original construction of Mandell and Rezk. This new definition 
is equivalent to the original, yet offers improved clarity and manageability. As a 
consequence, we also prove that the Mandell inverse K-theory of a monoidal category 
is closed under taking monoid morphisms. Finally, we provide an example of a category 
whose Mandell inverse K-theory is not stable under products. This research draws 
heavily from the original work of Mandell and Rezk. A revised version of the paper 
is available on arXiv:2206.01730. A subsequent paper will explore the Mandell 
inverse K-theory of monoidal 2-categories. This research is supported by NSF grant

We explore the Weyl algebra dual correspondence in the context of asymptotic three-dimensional spacetime. By applying the Dirac-Bergmann quantization method to the asymptotic symplectic structure, we derive the asymptotic Weyl algebra, and subsequently, the asymptotic Weyl dual copy, in which the asymptotic metric field is represented as a complex Weyl connection. This construction enables the description of asymptotic metrics in terms of Faddeev-Popov polynomials, whose first-order derivatives vanish. Notably, the resulting asymptotic Weyl copy exhibits a natural invariance to Lorentz transformations. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a unitary transformation mapping the phase space of General Relativity to that of the Weyl copy, and demonstrate that the Hamiltonian of the Weyl copy corresponds to the Hamiltonian of the metric field under this transformation. This result is extended to include Einstein-Hilbert and Chern-Simons theories. Finally, we examine the implications of the asymptotic Weyl copy for the holographic principle and discuss the possibility of deriving the Weyl copy from a first-order formulation of the effective theory on the boundary. This approach is also applied to the Chern-Simons theory, resulting in a connection representation of the effective theory. Notably, the resulting effective action exhibits a vanishing cosmological constant. This work provides a new perspective on the holographic principle, the Weyl copy, and the effective theory on the boundary, and offers a novel approach to the study of holography and gauge/gravity duality. revolutionize language learning and translation for under-resourced languages. The

Federated learning is an innovative approach to training machine learning models that respects user privacy by processing data locally. This approach is particularly useful in scenarios where users have limited data and want to leverage the strengths of their individual datasets. To achieve this, we introduce a new method called hyperwarp, which enables the creation of customized models by mapping the global model to a private dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that customized federated learning can outperform traditional methods in real-world applications, such as medical imaging, by adapting to individual user data. Furthermore, we show that hyperwarp can be more efficient than existing techniques by reducing the need for complex hyperparameter tuning. Our research provides a foundation for future studies on decentralized machine learning and data privacy. A significant issue in collaborative filtering is recommender systems' tendency to perpetuate filter bubbles, largely due to the reliance on the contrastive loss function. This research proposes a modified loss function, known as sensitive-margin loss, which incorporates bias-sensitive margins to address this issue. By doing so, sensitive-margin loss enables the model to learn from users with varying biases, effectively mitigating filter bubble creation. Furthermore, sensitive-margin loss can be seamlessly integrated into existing contrastive loss functions, making it a versatile solution. We introduce SMURF, a novel approach for unsupervised learning of optical flow that leverages a unique self-supervised framework. This framework enables the learning of complex, multi-frame optical flow from full-image, warping-based losses. Building on RAFT, our method incorporates a novel multi-frame training scheme that facilitates the learning of long-range flows. This is achieved through the development of a novel self-supervised loss function, which enables the training of a single model for multiple frames without relying on explicit multi-frame supervision. As a result, our approach can efficiently train models for up to 20 frames using a single model trained on single-frame data. Notably, our method outperforms leading state-of-the-art unsupervised optical flow algorithms, including PWC-Net, FlowNet2, and LDOF, on multiple benchmark datasets. high-quality, finely annotated datasets. The approach is built upon a deep
learning model and an interactive annotation tool, with the former producing
initial segmentations and the latter enabling experts to refine these results
via a dynamic, multi-scale, and multi-modal interface. The DIAL system is

producing high-quality, finely annotated semantic segmentation results. The
source code for DIAL is publicly available on GitHub under the handle

Go's lightweight concurrency model, combined with its growing popularity, makes it an attractive target for security analysis. However, the language's flexibility and lack of explicit concurrency enforcement features complicate static analysis. This research introduces BinGo, a static binary analysis tool that leverages machine learning to identify Go applications containing concurrency errors. By integrating information from various sources, including data flow, memory layout, and control flow, BinGo's neural network model detects potential concurrency issues. The tool's accuracy is evaluated through a comprehensive evaluation involving 12 Go programs with known concurrency bugs. The results demonstrate BinGo's ability to accurately identify a range of concurrency bugs, including data races, livelocks, and deadlocks, across various complexity levels. Furthermore, the study reveals that BinGo outperforms existing tools in both precision and recall, and it successfully identifies issues in real-world, open-source Go applications. In a multi-armed bandit scenario, we examine a unique situation where arm values change over time and are only revealed after each selection. We focus on sequences of arm selections that adhere to a monotone pattern, meaning that the order of selected arms either remains constant or increases consistently. We investigate the performance of a specific algorithm under this constraint and show that it can achieve near-optimal results in terms of both regret and the number of arm switches. Furthermore, we establish that near-optimal arm switches can be guaranteed even when arm values are unknown. We also demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms the standard Thompson sampling approach in this context. Finally, we conduct a simulation study to validate our theoretical claims and assess the algorithm's efficacy in real-world settings. The prediction of game outcomes in Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) games, such as League of Legends (LoL), is a complex task. To tackle this challenge, we developed a novel approach that leverages the synergy of various Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques. By extracting data from the LoL API, we can access information about player-champion pairings, player statistics, and game results. We then applied a range of NLP methods to analyze player-champion relationships, including text embedding, topic modeling, and sentiment analysis. Next, we combined these NLP features with player statistics from the game to create a comprehensive dataset. We used this dataset to train a Support Vector Machine (SVM) model, which we evaluated using a range of metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. Our model achieved an accuracy of 0.59, with a corresponding F1 score of 0.44. To further enhance our model's performance, we explored the use of different ML algorithms, including Decision Trees, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting, as well as neural networks. Our findings suggest that a combination of NLP and ML techniques can be a powerful tool for forecasting game results in LoL. To facilitate future research, we have made our code publicly available. Our work has the potential to inform the development of predictive models for other MOBA games, and we hope that it will inspire researchers to explore the application of NLP and ML in this field. To this end, we have identified several promising research avenues for future investigation. A widely used method for estimating causal effects through machine learning has been double machine learning (DML). Although DML has been successfully applied in various fields, including econometrics and public health, its use in causal mediation analysis has been limited until now. We also demonstrate the estimator's asymptotic properties and its robustness against model inaccuracies. Through simulations, we evaluate the estimator's performance under various scenarios and compare it with existing alternatives. Additionally, we apply this approach to a real-world dataset from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey to examine the relationship between body mass index and health outcomes, specifically cardiovascular disease risk, through the mediation of blood pressure. Our findings suggest that body mass index's effect on cardiovascular disease is significantly influenced by blood pressure. Furthermore, our approach offers greater efficiency and robustness against model inaccuracies compared to conventional linear regression-based mediation analysis. It also provides a more accurate estimation of body mass index's indirect effect than a widely used alternative based on ordinary least squares. Overall, our double machine learning-based estimator offers a more accurate estimation of causal mediation effects than existing methods. We outline the process of creating this new dataset, which draws from Government Documents One and expands its scope to include a broader range of files from 2015 to 2020. Ultimately, we believe that NapierOne offers a more suitable substitute for Government Documents One and can serve as a valuable resource for IR research. Recent research has focused on understanding the validity of feature attribution methods used to explain model predictions. Existing studies have primarily concentrated on evaluating these methods based on their accuracy and robustness. However, these assessments often overlook the fact that feature attribution methods are typically used in real-world applications, where models are frequently updated and changed. In this study, we introduce a new measure of robustness specifically designed to evaluate feature attribution methods in the context of models that undergo modifications. We also develop a new algorithm that leverages this measure to optimize feature attribution methods and demonstrate its effectiveness through both theoretical and experimental analysis. Our results show that this measure effectively captures the impact of model changes on feature attribution methods and enables the identification of the most robust methods. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that feature attribution methods optimized using this measure produce more accurate and robust explanations compared to existing methods. The code and data used in this study are available online. The findings of this study are expected to contribute to the development of more reliable and robust feature attribution methods that can withstand changes in the underlying models.
